Aerial Wildlife Survey Report  
Wildlife Management Unit 347 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2018-19) 
Background 
 
The Marsh Head Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 347 in the Upper Athabasca Region covers an area of 
1,580km2. WMU 347 is bordered by the Athasbasca, Little Smokey and Berland rivers, along with Highway 43 and 
two industrial roads known as the Fir and Big Stone roads. Other significant features include Smoke Lake, the 
towns of Fox Creek and Whitecourt and the Alexander First Nation Reserve (No. 134A) .  
 
This unit consists of 85% Lower Foothills, 9% Upper Foothills and 6% Central Boreal Mixedwood natural 
subregions. Coniferous forest makes up most of the unit (50%); with deciduous forests comprising 13% and 
shrubs, recent cutblocks and recent burns comprising 18%. Key Wildlife Biodiversity Zones overlap 26% and the 
Grande Cache Grizzly Bear Range (BMA 2) covers 49% of the unit. WMU 347 is almost entirely (>99%) crown 
land and is extensively used for forestry and oil and gas purposes.  
 
A survey for moose was last conducted for WMU 347 in 2009-10 using a random stratified block methodology; see 
Table 1 for previous moose survey estimates. The objective of the 2018-19 survey was to assess the status of the 
moose population in WMU 347 by determining estimates for abundance, density and the age-sex composition. 
White-tailed deer, mule deer and elk populations were not estimated due to limited observations and poor 
detectability using aerial survey methods. Since the survey was conducted in February, during favourable snow 
cover conditions, that would achieve a reliable moose population estimate, we were not able to acquire meaningful 
antler class data on moose and deer as most males had dropped their antlers prior to this assessment.   
 
Survey Method 
An aerial moose survey was conducted on February 5 and 6, 2019 using distance sampling techniques (Buckland 
et al., 2001, 2010). A total of 67 north-south transects (survey effort = 508.11 kilometers; 11.1 hours) were flown. 
Additional effort was allocated in areas of known elk herds, based on previous sightings in the last 10 years, in an 
attempt to get an elk population estimate using a minmum total count methodology. All observed ungulates were 
classified by age class (adult or young of the year). Moose and elk were classified by age class (adult or young of 
the year) and the adults by sex (cow or bull). Deer were classified to age class only since, we could not distinguish 
between the sexes as antlers had begun to drop prior to the survey. Other sightings of sensitive or at risk species 
(i.e. sharp-tailed grouse) or significant wildlife features (i.e. large raptor nests, dens) were recorded.  
 
Results 
  
Moose 
A total of 161 moose were observed in 88 groups. The estimated density was 0.39 moose/km 2 (90% CI 0.30 – 
0.51) and the estimated abundance was 615 individuals (90% CI 468 – 809). The coefficient of variation for both 
density and abundance was 0.167 (Table 2). A total of 160 moose were successfully classified and the 
bull:cow:calf ratio was estimated to be 37:100:54. A total of 43 calves were observed in 36 groups with 25% of

these groups having twins. The last three surveys show considerable overlap in the population estimate ranges at  
90% CI; though the mean estimates suggest a declining moose populat ion in this unit. However, this year’s survey 
did show a greater recruitment rate than the previous surveys.  
 
Elk and Deer 
A total of four white-tailed deer in 2 groups and 0 mule deer were observed during this survey, and only 30 elk in 2 
groups were observed even with additional search effort in areas of known elk herds. This low number of 
observations are likely attributed to  the thick forest canopy in this unit, and therefore are likely not be indicative of 
a limited deer or elk population. The narrow and irregular shape of this unit further inhibits our ability to determine 
an accurate elk population estimate as many of the elk herds transition between WMU 347 and the surrounding 
WMUs. For these reasons, we were not able to report a population estimate for elk or deer in this unit.
